prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose oeuvre that builds from memory, the body and dream an encyclopedic inner cosmos in Romanian.

statement.case_for: My opening view holds after reading my colleagues. The case for Cărtărescu rests on the oeuvre itself, not on how many of us placed him first. The public record of Blinding and Solenoid suggests a very distinctive voice and an unusually large formal ambition. Recurring image systems, parallel and nested structures, and the body, memory and dream are made into one sustained metaphysical project. Poetry and prose appear to belong to a single imaginative enterprise rather than a single peak. This also fits the criteria I use for every candidate: distinctiveness of voice, linguistic and formal achievement, intellectual depth and sustained quality. A citation can name the whole project as the creation of an interior cosmos in Romanian prose, and it need not rest on one title or on national symbolism. The late long-form novels suggest a consolidated oeuvre, so the timing question is less pressing than for candidates whose work is still being defined.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the case depends on prose whose density, rhythm and patterning I can only judge through translation. Maximalist, digressive long forms may read as depth to some readers and as repetition or excess to others. If the later volumes mainly extend the earlier image systems rather than deepening them, the claim of sustained quality across the whole body of work weakens. Coverage of the poetry and early work in translation is also thinner than for the major novels, so the citation could end up resting on a narrower sample than the oeuvre.

responses.point: Sward ranks Yoko Tawada second. She sees bilingual writing in Japanese and German as a formal principle across genres, and she notes that Cărtărescu's maximalist register may feel repetitive over very long forms.
responses.response: I take the repetition concern about Cărtărescu seriously. It is the real test of whether scale means depth or accumulation. I would want the committee to ask whether the long novels develop their image systems or only recirculate them, and I cannot settle that from translation alone. Tawada was not in my own top eight, so I cannot claim a comparison with confidence. Her case, as you put it, is a formal and linguistic one, and it needs assessment in both Japanese and German. It should not rest on a single translated line. I would want that corpus-coverage question answered before weighing her against the Romanian case.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg places Michon third for compressed, syntactically sculpted French prose, and ranks Can Xue last among the eight because the method stays the same over decades.
responses.response: I share your admiration for the sentence-level achievement in Michon, whom I ranked fourth. For a lifetime citation I still weigh the compact corpus against significance across a body of work, and I think the committee must discuss that openly. On Can Xue I am less negative than you, since I ranked her fifth. The sameness of method can be read as rigor or as limited development, and I cannot resolve that from the partial translated corpus. I would not dismiss her on that ground alone. I also would not move her above the leading candidates without better evidence of range.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Anne Carson second. She values the hybrid forms and the unmistakable voice, but warns that genre-crossing makes the scope of a citation harder to define.
responses.response: I agree with the qualification and it is why Carson is my first alternative and not my preference. Autobiography of Red and Nox show real formal invention and emotional force. A citation would have to rest on the original poetic work, with the scholarship and translation as context only. I would add that part of the force of the book-objects depends on their physical design, which complicates comparing them with a prose oeuvre. Whether the hybrid forms fit Nobel's will is for the committee to argue on the texts.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Can Xue second and describes an uncompromising method of dream logic and abandoned causality, while asking whether uniformity is rigor or repetition.
responses.response: You ask the right question, and the answer should shape how the committee reads Can Xue and Cărtărescu alike. I would apply the same test to both. Is the consistency of the method a deepening, or only a repetition of it? For Cărtărescu there is a visible arc from the poetry through the Blinding sequence to Solenoid, and that arc is why I place him higher. For Can Xue, partial translation prevents me from judging whether the arc exists. I do not conclude it does not.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's linguistic achievement survives translation. Romanian prose rhythm and density cannot be judged directly from the supplied evidence.
Translation coverage of the poetry and the early work is uneven, so the full corpus is not verified.
Whether the late long novels deepen the earlier image systems or mainly repeat them.
How the committee should weigh a compact oeuvre (Michon) or hybrid book-objects (Carson) against a large-scale prose project under the criterion of significance across a body of work.
The poetry of Adonis and the bilingual work of Tawada depend heavily on languages and forms that I cannot assess directly, and I have not independently verified any source.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My own practice, with its parallel narratives, myths and fairy tales, is context and not evidence of any preference. My documented connections (Lagerlöf, Kate Larson, David Håkansson, committee colleagues) do not involve any shortlisted writer.
